answer.rationale: The competitor's entry pricing creates pressure to match with promotional_pricing, but memory_73 is the one inherited record that carries an explicit downstream cost: a 31% new-account and 18% revenue lift bought with a 12-point renewal drop, and it was already marked unsuitable for repeat use. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, that is a direct disqualifier, not a tradeoff to re-litigate with a one-week slot; matching on price would also concede the pricing frame to the competitor. The two measured declines this quarter are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and completion is plausibly upstream of activation, so a single intervention at the onboarding step can address both. memory_86 (shortening onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value) and memory_31 (cutting required signup fields lifted first-week activation) converge on that step, which is why I am spending both verification pulls there rather than on memories I do not intend to act on. memory_91 (activation messaging) is the closest alternative and stays queued if verification weakens the onboarding record; memory_44 argues enterprise should keep its sales-assisted path, so any simplification must be scoped to the self-serve SMB funnel and must not divert demo-request traffic. Key downstream risk: fewer required fields and a shorter flow can raise raw signups while degrading qualification data and lead quality, converting a real activation lift into unqualified volume, so success must be measured on qualified activation and early retention rather than completion rate alone. Standing caveats on the inherited record: these results are 15-64 days old, predate the competitor's move, and the archived summaries do not state whether the observed lifts persisted past the first term, so I am running this as a standard instrumented experiment rather than a broad rollout.
